chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa ibn Ubayd from Yasin al-Darir who said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Abdillah narrated to me who said:

I said to the Sheikh (Al-Shaykh al-Saduq), 'Inform me about a man who claims a right against another man, but he has no evidence for what he claims.' He said, 'The oath is upon the defendant; if he swears, he has no right (to the claim), and if he does not swear, the right is upon him. And if the one against whom the right is sought has died, and evidence is established against him, then the oath is upon the claimant, swearing by Allah, the One there is no god but He, that so-and-so has died and indeed his right is upon him. If he swears, then fine; otherwise, he has no right, because we do not know, perhaps he had paid him with evidence whose location we do not know, or without evidence before death. From this, the oath becomes upon him along with the evidence. If he claims and has no evidence, he has no right, because the defendant is not alive. And if he were alive, he would be compelled to swear or give the right, or return the oath to him; from this, no right is established for him against him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on an oath when a claimant has no evidence against a deceased defendant?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the procedural mechanics of *al-yamin* (judicial oath) in civil disputes, emphasizing the principle that the burden of proof lies with the claimant while the oath serves as a secondary validation. It specifically addresses the nuance of deceased defendants, where the claimant must swear to the debt's existence due to the uncertainty of prior settlement, reflecting the Shia juristic focus on preserving rights (*haqq*) amidst evidentiary gaps. The text underscores the logical deduction that if the defendant were alive, they would be compelled to swear or pay, thus shifting the evidentiary weight when they are no longer present to testify.
